summary: Follow-up to RFC 392, which reported measurements of network use at Utah. The author says that RFC was meant to point out places the network could improve, not to simply criticise it, and hopes more measurement experiments will be done on other computers and operating systems.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 557 clarifies the purpose of an earlier network measurement report and presents improved TENEX transfer measurements from BBN. It argues that measurement can show where software needs work and asks other sites to report their results.

how did the tenex transfer measurements change
subtitle: A follow-up report on measurements of TENEX network-transfer performance.

tldr.problem: The author says RFC 392's measurements were read as criticism of the network, although its purpose was to identify opportunities to improve it. Few other measurement results had been reported.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC shares BBN's updated TENEX measurements after changes to the RJS program, input/output code and network monitor code.
tldr.outcome: The reported CPU time fell from 75–85 seconds per megabit to 19 seconds per megabit. The author asks other systems to measure and share their transfer results.

today: RFC 557 is a 1973 report of TENEX network-transfer measurements and a request for measurements from other systems.

sections.title: Why the Author Revisits RFC 392
sections.content: RFC 392 described a problem encountered while using the ARPANET at Utah. Its author says the goal was to point out a place for improvement, but readers seemed to treat it as a claim that the network was poor. RFC 557 also renews the request for measurements on computers and operating systems beyond TENEX.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier report was meant to help improve network use, not simply condemn the network. The author asks people using other computers to measure their own systems too.

sections.title: BBN's Updated TENEX Measurements
sections.content:
BBN updated Don Allen's RJS program to use recent TENEX changes, improved code near the input/output calls and used faster network monitor code. The resulting measurement was about 19 seconds of CPU time per megabit, compared with 75–85 seconds before. The RFC describes this as an approximately 400% improvement.

Of the 19 seconds, 13 were spent in RJS and 6 in TENEX network output. Separate BBN FTP measurements required 8.2 CPU seconds per megabit for 8-bit-byte transfers. The RFC says using 32- or 36-bit bytes improved that figure by a factor of four.
sections.plainLanguage: Changes to TENEX and its transfer programs reduced the measured CPU time per megabit. The report separates time spent in the RJS program from time spent in TENEX network output.

sections.title: The Call for More Measurements
sections.content:
The author says the results suggest the network, including the host cost, can be effective. Poor results may follow when monitor and user code are not carefully implemented. The report does not investigate where the remaining 13 seconds in RJS were spent, because RJS was expected to be replaced by an RJE protocol using FTP for transfer.

The author asks sites to measure network transfers and send results, including results they may find embarrassing.
sections.plainLanguage: The report says implementation choices affect measured transfer cost, and leaves part of the RJS cost unexplained. It asks other sites to measure their transfers and share what they find.
